A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PIA/VAE recommender study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite appendix reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, an Amazon streaming-platform A/B experiment, user-group analyses and an encoder-architecture comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains the benchmark and online results and adds original hyperparameter-sensitivity and training-time measurements.

M1.justification: v1 Algorithm 1 initializes, composes and trains invertible transformations, with a normalizing-flow extension defined in Appendix D.2. v2 removes those operations and the extension, leaving direct encoder sampling. This substantially simplifies the documented procedure; the anchor-alignment objective and adaptive weighting remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Both evaluate MovieLens-20M, Netflix and Million Song recommendation, the same Amazon streaming-platform deployment, and the same activity-based user groups. The new sensitivity and timing experiments use existing coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparison methods in Tables 1–3 remain unchanged. Deleting v1 Table 6 removes the supplementary comparisons against unaligned shallow, deeper and IAF encoders, including their corresponding aligned variants.

E3.justification: v2 introduces supplementary protocols sweeping alignment strength, patience and scaling, plus average seconds-per-epoch measurements. These replace the encoder-depth/flow experimental controls. The retained benchmarks preserve their data splits, ranking metrics, optimizer, batch size and 200-epoch budget.

E4.justification: v1's posterior-flexibility study comparing shallow, deeper and IAF encoders is removed. v2 Appendix D instead tests sensitivity to alignment strength and its scheduling parameters through Figures 3–6, and measures alignment's computational overhead. This substantially changes the supplementary questions investigated.

E5.justification: v1 describes the online improvements as significant without numerical statistical support. v2 reports p-values of 0.000 and Bayesian probabilities of positive improvement of 1.000 for click rates and 0.997 for playtime, describing a Normal-Normal historical prior. Neither version supplies repeated-run uncertainty for the offline scores.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and Figure 2 retain their results, but the supplementary findings change substantially. v1 Table 6's architecture results, including IAF nDCG@100 of 0.431 without alignment and 0.437 with alignment, disappear. v2 adds sensitivity results and training times of 8.207 versus 9.516 seconds on MovieLens-20M and 22.193 versus 25.722 seconds on Netflix.

T1.justification: The central definitions, theorems, propositions and Appendix E proofs remain substantively unchanged. v2 removes the normalizing-flow transformation, transformed-posterior objective and density equations from v1 Appendix D.2, Equations 11–13. Subsequent equation renumbering introduces no further theoretical change.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and principal conclusion retain the same claims about latent proximity, KL-versus-masking trade-offs, training-only personalized item alignment, benchmark benefits and successful online deployment.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of anchor geometry for diverse or multimodal users and of warm-user item neighborhoods helping cold users. It also states that excessive masking noise can defeat alignment. Conversely, it removes v1's interpretation that alignment effectiveness depends on posterior flexibility and that normalizing flows address the flexibility/collapse trade-off.

D1.justification: v1's explicit encoder/decoder dimensions, deeper and IAF architecture specifications, and universal alignment-weight setting of 8 disappear. v2 adds AWS ml.g5.2xlarge/A10G hardware, timing information, tuning ranges and the online experiment's 50/50 allocation. This materially changes reproducibility documentation, while the code link and basic training settings remain.

R1.justification: The removed flow discussion takes out citations to Dai et al. (2019), Kingma et al. (2016), Rezende and Mohamed (2015), and Tabak and Turner (2013). Santambrogio (2015) replaces Rubinstein (1970) as the transport-duality reference. Appendix B and the central novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify neighborhood transfer, gradient influence and Results 1–3. Appendices C–D are reorganized, with Algorithm 1 moved into implementation details. Publication-header, affiliation and terminology edits accompany these changes, while the main section sequence and much of the prose remain stable.

P2.justification: v2 adds paired validation/test heatmaps in Figures 3–5 and a multimetric sensitivity plot in Figure 6. The architecture-comparison Table 6 is removed and its number reused for a new runtime table. Existing Figures 1–2 and Tables 1–5 retain their content but are repositioned; the supplementary visual presentation changes substantially.

improvement.justification: v2 provides direct evidence for previously asserted hyperparameter robustness, quantifies training overhead, and better documents statistical support for the existing online experiment. Clearer explanations and an explicit masking limitation also help interpretation. These yield a modest net improvement, tempered by the loss of architecture specifications and the posterior-flexibility study; the central results and proofs remain unchanged.
